turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I hate how I'm being treated by my boyfriend. When we're out he'll tell me what to wear, what to say, even what to eat, and it makes me feel like I'm constantly doing wrong.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really sorry you're going through that. How is it affecting you day to day, and are you safe to talk right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It's like I'm in a box. I can't breathe, I'm constantly second-guessing, and it just exhausts me. He's not violent, it's more controlling.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds draining and suffocating. When does it feel the worst—out in public, at home, other times?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: It's in public mostly—out, in the car, even at his family's house. He tells me what to eat, what to wear, what to say. It feels like I'm always wrong.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for explaining. When he controls choices like that, do you feel like you lose your voice, or that he minimizes or dismisses your feelings?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah. I try to tell him I want to do my own thing, and he says I'm being selfish and that I'll regret it. He'll call me rude or unkind to friends, even if I didn't say anything.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a lot to carry. What do you hope for from this—more independence, less stress, or both? Do you feel okay sharing any support, like therapy or a counseling hotline?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I just want to feel like myself again. I don't know if I can do this with him. It feels like I'm always wrong, and I'm scared to say anything.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You deserve to feel yourself. Even a small step can help—like making one choice your way or writing down what you want. We can also talk about setting boundaries or grounding exercises if you want.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Maybe. I could try picking what I wear or what I eat for dinner, but I’m nervous he’ll push back. I just want him to stop telling me what to do.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It’s okay to start with the smallest choice you can control. You could also ask for one “your choice” without consequences—like, “If I choose a shirt, can we skip arguing about it?” Be clear about how you want to be treated.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I’m scared he’ll call me selfish or make it my fault. I also don’t want to get in a fight at family stuff. I’m stuck between wanting freedom and feeling safe.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That tension makes sense. You can focus on your boundaries: say, “I want to try this my way. If I mess up, I’ll figure it out.” You don’t have to justify every step. If the pressure is high, you can also lean on friends or a support line for practical help.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Thanks. I’ll try making one choice my own tonight and see how he reacts. I’ll also look up a counseling hotline if it helps.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi. My name is [Name], and I'm here because I've been really struggling. I was recently diagnosed with an eating disorder that I'm working on healing from.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for sharing that with me. I'm glad you're here. How have you been feeling lately, and when did the urges start showing up for you?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm a senior in high school, and since I started dating someone he's been pushing me to lose weight—his idea, not mine. He makes comments and even tells me that I have to lose weight, and that I should eat less.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That sounds really hard to carry. When he says those things, how do you respond, and do you ever feel pushed to do something specific?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I keep trying to brush it off because I don't want to argue, but he really pushes and I feel like I have to lose weight—his idea. My parents are really supportive and want me to do things like eating meals together and eating more healthy. But when I do that he doesn't like it and wants me to eat less.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: That’s a tough push-pull. When he criticizes you for eating more, what happens? Do you feel defensive, anxious, or pressured to hide how much you've eaten?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, he criticizes me for eating more and that I should eat less, and when I do, it makes me feel bad and I feel like he's controlling me. I don't want to lose weight, but his constant comments and pressure really make me think about it.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really sorry you're going through that. I'm here to help you figure out ways to protect yourself and your health. Would you be open to making a plan—like setting clear boundaries with him, choosing what to eat, and keeping meals with your parents—while also looking at the eating disorder part?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I want to protect myself and my health, but he keeps telling me I need to lose weight and it keeps getting in my head. I don't know if I'm losing weight because I want to or because he's been pushing me.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: It makes sense your head keeps spiraling. We can try grounding and coping steps for when the urges show up—things like slow breathing, a short grounding exercise, and choosing a simple meal plan that feels right for you. Also, I can refer you to therapy so we can work on your eating disorder in a supportive space.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm scared if he knows I'm going to therapy he'll stop talking to me. I don't know how to tell him I don't want to lose weight and I want to eat more healthy without him getting upset.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: You don't have to tell him everything. You could say it's for your mental health and that you're trying new habits. If he insists, we can also make a small boundary plan and discuss consequences. And if he says harmful things, it can help to save those comments and let me know.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can try saying it's for my mental health. I want to eat more healthy with my parents, but I feel bad if he doesn't like it. I also don't know what to do when he says I should eat less.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can work on a short script for when he criticizes you, like: “I’m focusing on my mental health and eating more healthy with my family. I’m not going to argue.” And a plan for your day—simple meal prep, grounding steps when urges hit, and reaching out to me so I can support you.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: That sounds doable. Can we start with a script and a meal plan, and also set up therapy so I can get help while standing up for myself?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Hi. I'm 14 and I need to report something about my friend. He keeps cutting his arms and it freaks me out.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm glad you told me. Is he safe right now, and how old are you and him?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I'm 14, he's 13. He cuts on his arms, and it scares me. I know it's not okay.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Thank you for being honest. Do you know why he does it, and what you've seen?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: He cuts because he feels like he's a bad person. I've seen his arms and they're covered in long, deep cuts—like he's been doing it for a long time—and I know he cuts on his arms.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I'm really glad you told me. I need to ask for your permission and follow the reporting process. Is there any immediate risk to him right now?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: No immediate danger that I know of. I'm just worried and feel helpless.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I hear you. We can take this to the school counselor and, if appropriate, also connect him with a school-based therapist. Would that be okay?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Yeah, I think that could help. I want him to get the help he needs.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: Good. I'll contact the counselor and arrange a meeting with him. Would you be willing to talk with him as well about not hurting himself?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: I can try. I just don't want it to get worse.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: We can go at his pace. While we connect him with support, can you also keep an eye on him for signs like worsening cuts, signs of infection, or any mention of not wanting to be here?

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Okay. I'll watch for that and let you know if I see anything.

turns.speaker: Listener
turns.text: I appreciate that. We'll keep you updated and make sure he has support. If anything changes or you feel unsafe, please let me know right away.

turns.speaker: User
turns.text: Alright. Thank you for listening and helping.
